speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The library is a common ground where diverse groups of people come together, be it young children eagerly browsing picture books at the children's corner, or students in reading rooms preparing for their examinations, or the elderly engrossed in their daily newspapers – the library is an identifiable icon in our cities and in our hearts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, as Singapore progresses to a Smart Nation, so must our libraries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I commend the efforts by NLB to upgrade our libraries to adopt the technologies of audio-visuals while preserving print books.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was delighted to see how Yishun library was transformed after its renovations earlier this year, to include digital learning zones, quick response (QR) code borrowing systems and more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also understand that within the Bill, amendments are made to the Copyright Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Under section 113 of the Copyright Act, cinematographic film and sound recordings are now included as online material that will be collected by NLB.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These materials will also be made available within the premises of the library.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the interests of publishers will be guaranteed to ensure that the sales of their hard work are not affected by the digital access provided by NLB?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Is there a grace period after publication before content will be made available in the libraries?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, web archiving is a practice observed in other countries, such as the British library, as the Minister mentioned, and the National Library of South Korea.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both the British and Korean libraries also have their web archives made available for public access.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the same vein, will all our web archives, without exclusions or exemptions, be made available for public access on NLB’s Web Archive Singapore portal or on other platforms?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Web content that is available today may not be as easily located or may even be taken off decades later.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With a proper database of Singapore-specific websites and content, it will be easier for academics, researchers and businesses to conduct research on Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Prof Ang Peng Hwa from the Wee Kim Wee School, also suggested to have indices and abstracts of archives made available online for citizens and researchers to have greater access.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While the Raffles Library was an exclusive book club that limited its access and membership to the elite, the NLB now serves all residents in Singapore through its 26 public libraries and national archives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As part of the process of preserving our national heritage and identity, the National Library Act mandated that two copies of every Singapore publication made available for sale or distribution should be deposited with the National Library for the purpose of posterity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This was mentioned by the Minister earlier on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These materials are invaluable in providing us with records of how our society’s narratives and discourses have evolved over the years, and how such narratives have shaped and continue to shape our community, our society and, indeed, our country.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In 1995, the Library Review Committee identified technology as a game changer that will disrupt the operations of libraries.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order for libraries to remain relevant and continue to serve the needs of the nation, the Committee recommended that NLB embrace technology and consider how technology could be used to promote and enhance the establishment of Singapore as an international information hub.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Committee's recommendations were prescient, as technology has, indeed, changed the way information is published, disseminated and stored.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more information gets published online and with physical copies of books giving way to electronic publications, the process of archiving information becomes challenging.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to re-examine how we can continue in our quest to preserve parts of our history and identity in the digital age, or risk social amnesia where important electronic information is lost due to the lack of means to archive them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Minister mentioned earlier, NLB currently relies on two main ways to archive online content.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, NLB would seek explicit consent from owners of websites to take a snapshot of their sites and archive those snapshots in a restricted access database.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One of the key benefits of the amendments is to allow NLB to create a more complete picture about online discourses, especially those that shape social or political narratives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The open nature of the Internet allows for more pluralistic expressions of opinions and views.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With more conversations taking place on online platforms like blogs, websites, forums and social media, it makes sense for us, as a nation, to archive those conversations so that our future generations can gain access to important records about how their social or political landscape has been shaped by the generations before them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While most people would agree that we need to preserve websites and digital materials for records and posterity, we need to consider several aspects of this practice.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, with new websites and digital content being published or created daily, the amount of information that NLB needs to manage could be increasingly large.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With such a wealth of information, how would NLB ensure that the information is stored securely while yet remaining publicly accessible?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And while the Bill has made provisions for the archival information to be made accessible, can we consider easing the rules of how this archived content could be accessed and used so that more people can benefit from them?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: NLB, in this instance, needs to clarify and explain the boundaries of public and private copyrights, and how it intends to protect private copyright and IP when digital copies of such e-publications are made publicly accessible.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such expressions of thought are important reflections of our community and I agree with the amendments to the Act that will allow such e-publications and websites to be archived.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The proliferation of digital media means that more and more content is being generated by a more diverse range of sources.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Anyone can create a blog, write a post or self-publish an e-book online.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This has several implications for NLB's archival functions.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: First, focusing on traditional sources is not enough.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This updates the intent of the Act fit for our modern circumstance.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: However, how does NLB define the scope of online material which may be web-harvested?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Will it be clear to the content creators whether each particular piece of content would qualify to be web-harvested?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Do they have the right to reject web-harvesting?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And if web-harvesting applies only to "Singaporean websites", would this create an incentive to post content on overseas sites, with the deliberate intent to avoid archiving?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The ephemeral nature of the Internet means that old content may disappear forever.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This archive may be the only place that future researchers will be able to access such content.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Websites are updated daily, sometimes even more than once a day.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How much could be lost between each archiving exercise?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But unless NLB is Google, it would be impossible to archive the entire Internet constantly.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, a line will need to be drawn.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The question is whether annual is the right line.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Conversely, having collected such a comprehensive catalogue of materials, how will NLB use and make accessible the electronic publications and archived websites so that more people can benefit from valuable content about our country?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have to be conscious of the need to balance the public interest with that of the copyright holders and ensure that access to the material is controlled.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Copyright Act is being amended to enable the content to be archived without violating copyright.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is, of course, critical to protect the rights of content creators but, at the same time, it is in the national interest to allow access to the treasure trove of archived documents.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is similar to the offering in other countries, such as the UK, where there is one user per legal deposit library, and New Zealand, which allows only three users at a time.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But does this achieve the right balance between the need for access and the protection of copyright?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: How did the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI) determine the number and location of access terminals?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For example, should researchers at universities be allowed to access the materials with some safeguards?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Also, how would users who are unable to travel physically to the NLB site access the data?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Should some level of online access be allowed, but carefully tracked to avoid abuse?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In fact, one may argue that the speed with which content is created means that the value of "old" news decays faster online than it does in the print world.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In that case, perhaps the balance of the Act should be settled in favour of the user rather than the copyright holders.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After all, it would take great determination to wait a year to queue up at two terminals to read content.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The other facet of the Internet is the diversity of views, which can be published online without any filters or approvals.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Compared to the old days of publishing, there is likely to be a lot more controversial content – content of low quality or accuracy, or downright threats to our national security.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The furore around Fake News in Singapore and around the world is a testimony to the pervasiveness of this phenomenon.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: What will NLB do about websites with objectionable content, for example, content which could pose a threat to national security?

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While it seems that the NLB should archive these for the sake of posterity, what safeguards will be put in place to restrict access?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon has asked about the scope of online material which may be web-harvested, and whether it would be clear to website owners which elements of their websites would be web-harvested.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This means that NLB will not be collecting material residing in social media, such as Facebook, Twitter and Instagram, that are not within the .sg domain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For .sg websites, NLB will archive all the pages within the websites, including images, portable document format (PDF) documents, audio files and video files, that are hosted within the websites themselves.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, content hosted on external websites, such as links to videos hosted on YouTube, will not be archived.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In addition to .sg domain websites, we also recognise that there are other non.sg websites which may also contain valuable content about Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For such websites, NLB will proactively approach the site owners for permission to archive the sites.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon has also asked if an annual web-harvesting exercise would be sufficient, given that the content on the Internet changes so quickly and frequently.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do not intend to emulate Google, I assure Mr Ong, but the proposed frequency of harvesting the .sg domain websites is generally in line with international practices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: However, as I mentioned earlier, there will be instances where some websites will be archived more frequently.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it becomes a judgement call in terms of the currency and relevance.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But by and large, an automated annual exercise should suffice to provide that snapshot that is being sought.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On the specific issue of whether NLB will be web-harvesting objectionable material, such as content which could pose a threat to Singapore’s national security, to be clear, what NLB endeavours to do is to preserve a comprehensive record of Singapore-related websites through web-harvesting.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As these are important resources that chart Singapore's cultural and social changes over time, it is essential that we capture them as they are so that they can accurately reflect the cultural and social landscape of our nation at different points in time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In other words, NLB will still archive the content, but may not allow access to it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Ong Teng Koon has also asked if website owners could decline to be web-harvested.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: He also pointed out that some website owners might post their content on non .sg sites to avoid being archived.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In general, if you are publishing content on a website, one assumes that you want it to be read, and it is counter-intuitive to then say that "I want it to be published but I do not want it to be archived".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, our public consultation with website owners last year showed that they were generally receptive and supportive of the web-harvesting initiative as they understood that the intent is for us to retain the collective memories of our nation.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Furthermore, this will allow them to have their content captured and stored for posterity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I think it is an alignment of interest.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We recognise that website owners have the right to choose the platforms on which they distribute their materials, but we hope that they will join us in our efforts to keep a part of our history alive.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Several Members, Mr Louis Ng in particular, had also asked how NLB would be ensuring that publishers' rights and content creators' copyrights and IP are protected, while making collected material easily accessible to people.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: All three Members asked whether we can consider making access to digital archived content more accessible, so that more people can benefit from them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Indeed, it is important that we ensure that the nation's published heritage is accessible to future and current generations of Singaporeans, and for all the good reasons that we have emphasised.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But at the same time, we also share their concerns regarding the protection of commercial interests of publishers of electronic materials, and they have asked how we will ensure that these interests will not be compromised in any way through the amendments to this Act.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We have also heard these concerns from stakeholders, like book publishers, in our consultations.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These materials can only be viewed at the computer terminals with no downloading, copying or printing allowed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Two concurrent users will be able to view each item in the collections at any one time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This approach mirrors that of NLB's current Legal Deposit policy for physical materials, which requires two copies to be deposited.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We think this strikes a good starting balance between safeguarding publishers' IP interests and giving public access to these materials.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are, however, instances where the content of the collected electronic materials or websites are made available to the public beyond the library's premises.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is now done where express permission has already been given by the copyright owner or when the copyright has expired, and the content will be made accessible via NLB's digital services and websites, such as BookSG and Web Archives Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, the archived websites of the W!ld Rice Theatre Company (www.wildrice.com.sg), the Eurasian Association Singapore (www.eurasians.org.sg) and Singapore National Olympic Council (www.singaporeolympics.sg) are made available online as prior consent has been given, while the digitised copy of Hikayat Abdullah (Stories of Abdullah), published by the Mission Press in 1849, is also available online as the copyright has expired.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In the event that members of the public or researchers wish to use the content beyond just research and study, they will still have to approach the copyright owners for permission.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked if there was a grace period after publication before content will be made available in the National Library.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For instance, in the case of websites, it may take up to six months from the last archiving exercise before a website is ready for public viewing.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The online material collected via web-harvesting will also be made available in an easily accessible form.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if NLB will be making indices and abstracts of archives available online for citizens and researchers to have greater access.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am very happy to share with him that NLB is at present already cataloguing and indexing websites for which they have obtained permission to archive.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Archived websites can be found on NLB's digital platform One Search, and their Web Archives Singapore has an alphabetical and subject listing of all archived websites to date.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As Mr Darryl David has pointed out, there is a large amount of information collected via Legal Deposit and Web Harvesting which NLB needs to ensure is stored securely while remaining publicly accessible.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On this point, I want to highlight that NLB has a secure digital infrastructure that is protected in accordance with robust Government standards.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There are regular reviews of the security and resilience of our system, including the necessary firewalls and antivirus software, to protect against malicious cyber activities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Alongside this, NLB’s digitisation and preservation policies will ensure that deposited content is preserved.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: These amendments are especially crucial in this digital era, given that more and more valuable materials are now residing online and available in electronic formats.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We must focus our collection efforts on such materials now so that we do not lose important pieces of our culture, heritage and history.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On this note, I want to once again thank all three Members who have spoken in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.00 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.36 pm until 4.00 pm.
